rashi:a1.1: Permitted: because the reason [of Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam] is that it is an unintended act.
rashi:a2.1: Mesokhrayya denazyata: the spigot of a barrel, around which they wrap tow and rags so that it seals the hole well.
rashi:a2.2: It is prohibited to insert it tightly: into the barrel with force, because of squeezing. And even though he does not intend any squeezing, it is prohibited even according to Rabbi Shimon, who says in tractate Shabbat (41b) that an unintended act is permitted.
rashi:a3.1: And will it not die: since he presses it in tightly, it is impossible without squeezing. But clearing the hair is possible without plucking.
rashi:a4.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: evidently Rav holds that an unintended act is prohibited.
rashi:a4.2: Without men: without Rav Ḥiyya and Rav Ḥanan [the transmitters].
rashi:a5.1: And plucking is not shearing: that is why Rav said the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei [ben HaMeshullam] regarding the firstborn.
rashi:a5.2: In an unusual manner: for the way is not to pluck wool but to shear it.
rashi:a6.1: One who plucks the wing: who plucks a large feather from the wing of a bird.
rashi:a6.2: And one who snips it: after plucking it, he snipped off its tip.
rashi:a6.3: And one who pulls it out: he smooths it from the sides and strips the down off the shaft.
rashi:a6.4: Shearing, cutting and smoothing are among the primary categories of labor listed in tractate Shabbat (73a). Memaḥek: smoothing.
rashi:a6.5: That is its normal way: for the way with a bird’s feather is to pluck it, not to shear it.
rashi:a7.1: From the fact that Rav holds like Rabbi Yosei: regarding the firstborn, that plucking is not shearing.
rashi:a7.2: Rabbi Yosei also holds like Rav: that an unintended act is prohibited.
rashi:a8.1: This is the correct reading: “their roots are red and their tops are black.” And so it is in the Tosefta of tractate Para (2:4).
rashi:a8.2: He shears: the top that is black, with scissors, and leaves the part from the red onward, and need not be concerned about shearing consecrated animals. Evidently, since he does not intend any shearing but only to repair [the heifer], it is permitted. Two hairs that are entirely black disqualify a heifer completely, but where their roots are red and their tops black, it can be remedied.
rashi:a9.1: That is not subject to shearing: cows have no wool; therefore it is not prohibited with regard to shearing.
rashi:a9.2: “You shall do no work… and you shall not shear”: the “and” adds to the first matter, so that the two are derived from each other.
rashi:a10.1: That it is consecrated for Temple maintenance: since it is not offered on the altar; therefore it is permitted to shear it.
rashi:a10.2: That is uncommon: and with something uncommon the Rabbis did not issue a decree.
rashi:a11.1: Its price is expensive: and its value is not so readily available to desacralize it onto.
rashi:a13.1: Lekofitz, “for a cleaver”: for the sake of the cleaver.
rashi:a14.1: Ab initio: [the dilemma is] whether it speaks ab initio, and this “and likewise” refers to plucking: just as it is permitted to pluck for the sake of slaughter, for it is obvious to you that the first clause speaks ab initio, so too to see the place of a blemish. Or whether it speaks after the fact, and this “and likewise” refers to “provided that he does not move it,” and this is what it says: and likewise one who plucked hair to see the place of a blemish must also not move it from its place.
rashi:a14.2: Entangled in the ear: and the blemish was in the ear.
rashi:a15.1: Whose slaughter renders it evident: that he did not intend shearing.
rashi:a16.1: Rather, isn’t it referring to plucking: and it speaks ab initio.
rashi:a17.1: Mishna. Permits: the wool, for benefit, to the priest.
tosafot:a2.1: Mesokhrayya denazyata: we explained it in the first chapter of Ketubot (6a, s.v. ha’i) and in Shabbat (111a, s.v. ha’i).
tosafot:a5.1: Because it is uprooting an item from its place of growth in an unusual manner: one should not learn from here that it is permitted to pluck feathers from the neck of a bird in order to slaughter it on a Festival. For above it was explained that the reason it is permitted here is that it is unintended. And also according to the version that explained [the permission as applying] even when intended, with feathers it is not an unusual manner, as is taught nearby regarding one who plucks [the wing of] a bird. And even though here he does not need the feathers, so that it is a labor not needed for its own sake, one cannot derive a labor not needed for its own sake from [the leniency of] an unusual manner.
tosafot:a6.1: And Reish Lakish says: liable due to shearing: this is puzzling. What is the objection? Even though with regard to a firstborn one is not liable for “you shall not shear,” with regard to Shabbat one would be liable for a subcategory of shearing, as with anything uprooted from its place of growth in living creatures. So it is in Ḥullin (73a): one who reached into an animal’s womb and detached the fetus inside it is liable with regard to Shabbat, yet with consecrated animals one is not liable for shearing. Similarly, plucking [kituf] is liable on Shabbat as a subcategory of reaping, and so too plucking from what is attached to the ground, even though plucking does not count [as reaping] with regard to reaping before the omer (Pesaḥim 11a), nor with regard to gleanings, in the chapter Reshit HaGez (Ḥullin 137a). Had we explained that the Gemara here objects to what was said, that plucking counts as an unusual manner, it would be fine: it brings proof from here that it is not an unusual manner. But the wording does not imply this, since it says “And is plucking not shearing? But isn’t it taught: One who plucks the wing…”, which implies that it objects to the statement that plucking is not shearing.
tosafot:a7.1: From the fact that Rav holds like Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam, Rabbi Yosei holds like Rav: who says an unintended act is prohibited. For if Rabbi Yosei held that an unintended act is permitted, how would Rav know to rule like him because plucking is not shearing? Perhaps Rabbi Yosei permits because an unintended act is permitted, and plucking is shearing. Rather, Rav was certain that Rabbi Yosei holds an unintended act is prohibited.
tosafot:a8.1: Their roots black and their tops red: so it was written in the books. One may explain that it mentions “their tops red” to teach a greater novelty: even though [the hair] is entirely red on the outside, it requires cutting. And the Kontres [Rashi] reads the reverse, based on the Tosefta of Para.
tosafot:a8.2: He shears with scissors and need not be concerned: that is, even if he shears other hairs unintentionally, and even these themselves, if he shears more than needed. According to the reading of the Kontres, “their tops black,” [the Gemara] would infer that he holds an unintended act is permitted. And in the Kontres he explained that the inference is from its being permitted because he does not intend any shearing but only to repair [the heifer]. But that is not like the usual sense of an unintended act elsewhere, since he shears with scissors intentionally. One may reconcile the Kontres’s explanation: the objection is this. Does Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam hold that an unintended act is prohibited, and permit [with the firstborn] only because plucking is not shearing? But we find with the heifer that even with scissors, which is shearing, it is permitted because he does it to render the heifer fit; then with the firstborn too he should have permitted it in every manner, since he does it to prepare the slaughter, and this is not considered shearing. However, this explanation does not seem right at all, since the objection could then be raised in any case, whether his reason is that an unintended act is permitted or that plucking is not shearing.
tosafot:a17.1: In brief: The hair of a blemished firstborn that shed: this whole passage shows that the shearings of disqualified consecrated animals are permitted by Torah law, and even the Rabbis who forbid them do so, as the Gemara explains, by a decree lest he delay [the slaughter]; and what was expounded above (6b), “you shall slaughter, and not shearing,” means “slaughter, and do not shear.” My teacher found this puzzling: in Ḥullin (36b), the verse “you shall pour it on the ground like water” comes to permit the blood of disqualified consecrated animals, since one might have thought that because they are forbidden in shearing and work their blood must be buried. How could one think to forbid the blood for that reason, when even the shearings themselves are permitted? If you answer that only wool that shed is permitted by Torah law, while intentional shearing is forbidden: first, blood [that flows by itself] is like shed wool; and second, they disagree even about plucking (26a), which shows the Rabbis forbid it only rabbinically; even with an unblemished burnt offering the shearings are forbidden only rabbinically, as is evident below regarding one who plucks wool from an unblemished burnt offering, and the question “one who plucks, is there anyone who permits it?” means rabbinically, as the Kontres explains there, because he is wicked. A further difficulty in Ḥullin: why is a verse needed to permit that blood for benefit at all? Even the blood of offerings is permitted for benefit once its mitzva is done, and where there is no mitzva, why would it be forbidden? And the reasoning “since they are forbidden in shearing and work” does not fit blood of slaughter, since from slaughter onward shearing and work are permitted; milk too is not forbidden after slaughter, according to the one who expounds (15b) “you have no permission to eat them except from slaughter onward,” and indeed by all opinions, as shown by the derivation of the permission of milk in chapter 1 (6b). One may answer that the verse “like water” is needed for blood that came out before most of the simanim were cut; but the difficulty from our passage remains. My teacher’s answer: one might have thought to forbid blood the way milk is forbidden, from “and you shall eat meat” (Deuteronomy 12:15), meaning meat and not milk or blood, even for benefit, though the derivation fits blood less well than milk. This is unlike shearing, which may derive from “you shall slaughter,” implying slaughter and not shearing. Ḥullin cites “you shall slaughter, and not shearing” rather than “meat and not milk” because it took the first item, and because it preferred the shearing prohibition, which carries lashes before the animal is slaughtered (as we learned: one who shears or works it receives forty lashes); since the Torah was so stringent there, one might have expounded “meat, and not milk or blood” stringently, were it not for “like water.” And so it is evident in chapter 1 (6b) that “meat and not milk” does not forbid the act of milking, since the Gemara there wished to infer the permission of milk of non-sacred animals from it; rather, the verse comes to forbid milk that has been milked. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b18.1: One who plucks wool from an unblemished firstborn: at the conclusion of our passage it is explained that “plucks” is not precise, for the same is true of wool that was plucked [by itself]. It mentions “plucks” only because of the latter clause, which teaches “plucks” to convey the novelty of Akavya’s view.
gershom:a1.1: And does Rav say this: that an unintended act is permitted?
gershom:a2.1: Mesokhrayya denazyata: the stopper of the barrel’s seal.
gershom:a3.1: It is prohibited to insert it tightly: to seal it, because of squeezing.
gershom:a4.1: Even Rabbi Shimon, who says an unintended act is permitted, concedes that it is prohibited.
gershom:a5.1: Rav says the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda: who says an unintended act is prohibited.
gershom:a6.1: In an unusual manner: that is, not for the sake of uprooting but for the sake of slaughter, since the usual way [with wool] is not uprooting but shearing.
gershom:a7.1: The wing: the feather of a bird.
gershom:a8.1: And snips it: as in “snips it in two.”
gershom:a9.1: And pulls it out: the feather from its shaft.
gershom:a10.1: Liable due to shearing: for it is a subcategory of shearing.
gershom:a11.1: That is the normal way of a wing, by plucking; but plucking wool is not its normal way, and it is not like shearing.
gershom:a12.1: Rabbi Yosei holds like Rav: who says an unintended act is prohibited.
gershom:a13.1: Two hairs: on a red heifer.
gershom:a14.1: Whose roots are red and whose tops are black.
gershom:a15.1: He shears: the black part with scissors, that is, in order to render it fit.
gershom:a16.1: And need not be concerned: about shearing consecrated animals, since an unintended act is permitted.
gershom:a17.1: A heifer is different, as it is not subject to shearing: that is why he need not be concerned; but in truth he holds that an unintended act is prohibited.
gershom:a18.1: The verse states: “You shall do no work… and you shall not shear”: “and you shall not shear” is expounded both with what precedes it and what follows it, and “you shall do no work” is derived from “you shall not shear.”
gershom:a19.1: But there is a rabbinic prohibition: so why does it say “and need not be concerned”?
gershom:a20.1: That is uncommon: for there were only seven of them in all, as we learned at the beginning of [tractate] Para, and the Rabbis did not decree about it; but in truth he holds that an unintended act is prohibited. And the Talmud responds: why shear it while the heifer is consecrated? Let him desacralize it onto money, take it out to non-sacred status, and shear it while it is non-sacred.
gershom:a21.1: Its price is expensive: and he does not have so much money to redeem it at its value.
gershom:a22.1: [A note on the text of Rabbeinu Gershom:] Our Rabbeinu’s reading in the Gemara has: “And if you wish, say: when the ox was included [in the prohibition of shearing], it was for shearing its tail” (see the Shita, letter 5): for shearing its tail, and not the rest of its body. [On this reading, a heifer is still not subject to shearing of its body.]
gershom:a23.1: With a cleaver: that is, he plucks it with the cleaver, which is a tool.
gershom:a24.1: Teach “for a cleaver”: that is, he plucks it by hand in order to make room for the cleaver.
gershom:a25.1: Ab initio or after the fact: for “one who plucks” implies ab initio [the printed text has been corrected from “after the fact”], since this “and likewise” is taught about plucking and implies ab initio; that is, just as it said “he clears space,” which speaks ab initio, so “and likewise one who plucks”: he plucks ab initio. Or perhaps this “and likewise” refers to “provided he does not move it,” meaning: and likewise one who plucks must also not move it from its place; but then we would still not know whether plucking is ab initio or after the fact.
gershom:a26.1: He plucks it and shows it: that is ab initio.
gershom:a27.1: Now, there, where the slaughter makes it evident that he is not doing it for the wool, you said he may not move it; with one who plucks to see the place of a blemish, where nothing makes it evident, since the blemish is not noticeable to people, is it necessary to say that he may not move it? Rather, conclude that this “and likewise” refers to plucking: he plucks ab initio, as with “he clears space.” Conclude from it.
gershom:a28.1: The hair of a blemished firstborn: its wool, some of which shed.
gershom:a29.1: And he placed it in a compartment: because its wool is entirely forbidden during its life, since disqualified consecrated animals are forbidden in shearing and work.
gershom:a30.1: And afterward he slaughtered it with its blemish, Akavya ben Mahalalel permits: just as slaughter permits everything, the meat and the hide and the wool on it, so too it permits this wool that shed.
rashi:b1.1: And the Rabbis prohibit: for if you permit wool that sheds during its life, he will come to keep the firstborn [alive] so that it sheds wool all the time, and will come to a stumbling block with it, that he will shear it or work it; and disqualified consecrated animals are forbidden in shearing and work, as we said in the chapter above (6b): “You shall slaughter,” and not shearing.
rashi:b1.2: It was not in this that Akavya permitted: the Gemara explains what he means.
rashi:b1.3: And afterward it died: it was not slaughtered.
rashi:b2.1: Dangling: torn loose from the skin, but entangled with the rest of the wool so that it does not fall.
rashi:b2.2: That which appears with the fleece: when he slaughters it and shears it after slaughter, the dangling wool will be level with the rest of the fleece and will not appear separated from it; it is permitted like the rest of the fleece.
rashi:b2.3: And that which does not appear with the fleece: it sticks out too far, and it is evident to all that it is separate from the fleece, like wool that shed completely before slaughter. And this unattributed ruling follows the Rabbis who disagree with Akavya.
rashi:b3.1: Gemara. By inference that he prohibits? [A question of astonishment.] Now, with a dead animal, where the wool attached to it is forbidden since it requires burial, wool that shed and lies in a compartment is permitted;
rashi:b3.2: If he slaughtered it: where the wool attached to it is permitted, is it necessary to say that the wool lying in the compartment is also permitted according to Akavya?
rashi:b4.1: Rather: this is why he said “it was not in this that Akavya permitted”: because of “and the Rabbis prohibit” [since in the slaughter case the Rabbis do not prohibit].
rashi:b5.1: Where an expert permitted it: the firstborn, before the wool shed. For the Rabbis hold that there is a decree: if you permit the wool for benefit, perhaps he will come to keep it [alive] so that wool sheds from it, and in the meantime he will come to shearing and work. Therefore, even though an expert permitted it, it is forbidden. And Akavya holds that since an expert permitted it, he will no longer delay it.
rashi:b5.2: All agree it is prohibited: for it is like an unblemished animal, and with an unblemished animal Akavya concedes, as we say below: if you say the wool is permitted, he will come to keep it so as not to sacrifice it, and this suits him, since in the meantime a blemish will occur in it and remove it from the sanctity of the altar. Furthermore, since an expert did not permit it before the shedding, there was not yet any aspect of permission in it.
rashi:b6.1: Render prohibited in any amount: if one of them became mixed with a thousand unblemished animals, all of them are forbidden for the altar.
rashi:b7.1: By inference the first tanna holds not? [A question of astonishment.] Since he recognizes it, what doubt is there?
rashi:b8.1: With the shearings of a blemished firstborn: that shed during its life and that he placed in a compartment.
rashi:b8.2: Let it be investigated: if it is a permanent blemish, let him slaughter it, and everything will be permitted.
rashi:b8.3: And Rabbi Yehuda holds there is no remedy through slaughter. Evidently, for the Rabbis according to Rabbi Yosei, who permit when it was slaughtered, there is no distinction between where an expert permitted it beforehand and where an expert did not, since here it teaches that it is still to be investigated. And since according to the Rabbis there is no distinction where it was slaughtered, for Akavya too there is no distinction with a dead animal between where they permitted it and where they did not, since Akavya does not distinguish between a dead animal and a slaughtered one.
rashi:b11.1: He stated this halakha: that of Rav Naḥman.
rashi:b11.2: The dispute: between the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei concerns actual living blemished animals that became mixed with others, where he examined and did not find the blemished one.
rashi:b12.1: It is forever: in its presumption of impurity. If the grave that was lost in the field was not found, even though the whole field was examined, it remains in its impurity. Here too, since the blemished animal was not found, all of them are forbidden. The first tanna is like Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yosei, who says “let it be investigated,” holds that this is enough even if it was not found, like the Rabbis.
rashi:b13.1: He digs: he examines until he reaches bedrock, for certainly no grave was made below that rock, since it is hard.
rashi:b13.2: Or virgin soil: until he finds hard ground that was never worked.
rashi:b14.1: Where he examined and found: the blemished animal. The first tanna, who forbids all of them, is concerned that perhaps the one that was found is a different blemished animal, and all the others require examination. And Rabbi Yosei holds “let it be investigated”: the investigation at the outset suffices, and since he found this one, there is no doubt. The first tanna is like Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel] and Rabbi Yosei is like Rabbi.
rashi:b16.1: Granted, with regard to impurity: the Rabbis say he examines until he reaches bedrock or virgin soil and that is enough, because even if he does not find it one can say a raven or a mouse took it. But here even the Rabbis would prohibit, for where would the blemished animal have gone? And in a case like this Rabbi Yosei would not permit.
rashi:b16.2: And the other: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba.
rashi:b17.1: Granted, a field: Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel] said let it be examined, since it is normal to bury in it, and so on.
rashi:b17.2: Is it normal for them to develop a blemish? [A question of astonishment.] And in a case like this the first tanna would not prohibit.
rashi:b17.3: And the other: Rav Asi. [The daf reads Rabbi Asi.]
gershom:b1.1: And the Rabbis prohibit: since it shed during its life, and disqualified consecrated animals are forbidden in shearing and work.
gershom:b2.1: Rabbi Yosei said to him, and so on: in this case Akavya ben Mahalalel permits: even though the wool on it requires burial, this that shed during its life is permitted; and the Rabbis prohibit.
gershom:b3.1: Now, with a dead animal, even though it requires burial with its wool, he permits what shed during its life; where he slaughtered it, so that its wool is permitted for benefit, all the more so what shed during its life is permitted.
gershom:b4.1: Rather, it was not in this that he permitted: that is, where it shed before slaughter both permit it, and they disagree only about a dead animal whose wool shed before its death.
gershom:b5.1: The dispute: according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that they disagreed about a slaughtered animal, and according to Rabbi Yosei, who holds that they did not disagree about a slaughtered animal, is where an expert permitted the blemished firstborn before its hair shed. For Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Rabbis hold that by right it should be permitted after slaughter, since it shed after an expert permitted it; but if you permit the hair that sheds, he will come to keep the blemished animal alive longer than the period the Sages set in the chapter below, thinking: every day some of its hair sheds, and I will collect it and have much wool; and he will not want to slaughter them, and perhaps he will come to a stumbling block, shearing it or working it unwittingly. Therefore the Rabbis prohibited hair that shed before slaughter. And Rabbi Yosei holds that they did not decree lest he delay; rather, once an expert permitted it and afterward it shed and he slaughtered it, even the Rabbis permit. But if an expert did not permit it before it shed, even Rabbi Yosei concedes that the Rabbis prohibit the hair that shed, even though he slaughtered it, for since it shed before an expert permitted it, it is considered as though it shed from it [while unblemished] and is forbidden.
gershom:b6.1: Blemished animals render prohibited in any amount: implying that if a blemished animal became mixed with a hundred unblemished consecrated animals, all of them are forbidden.
gershom:b7.1: And Rabbi [Yosei; the printed text, Asi, is corrected] says let it be investigated: which one is the blemished animal, and the rest are permitted.
gershom:b8.1: Here, this “blemished animals render prohibited in any amount” does not speak of an actual blemished animal; rather, we are dealing with the shearings of a blemished firstborn that became mixed with non-sacred shearings, and he slaughtered the blemished animal.
gershom:b9.1: And who is the first tanna, who says it is prohibited in any amount? Rabbi Yehuda. And Rabbi Yosei, who says let it be investigated, is the Rabbi Yosei of our mishna, who holds that where they were slaughtered the Rabbis permit.
gershom:b10.1: Is it not “let it be investigated”: if it is a permanent blemish and he slaughtered it, it is permitted, and if it is a temporary blemish its shearings are forbidden; so even though an expert did not permit it before the hair shed, it is permitted if it is a permanent blemish. This is difficult for Reish Lakish, who said that where an expert did not permit it before it shed, all agree it is forbidden.
gershom:b11.1: No, let it be investigated: the matter, whether an expert permitted it before it shed: if so, yes; if not, no.
gershom:b12.1: He stated this halakha: what Rav Naḥman answered about the shearings.
gershom:b13.1: The dispute: of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei is where he examined and did not find the blemished animal. They do not disagree about shearings but about the blemished animal itself, and there is no difficulty.
gershom:b14.1: And in the dispute of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis: [who say he digs] until he reaches bedrock, and then it is pure. Here too Rabbi Yosei says: since he investigated and did not find it, all are permitted; and the first tanna holds like Rabbi Meir.
gershom:b15.1: The dispute is where he examined: for that blemished animal and found it, and the first tanna is concerned that perhaps the one he found is not the one that became mixed among them but another, and the one that became mixed has not yet been found; therefore all are forbidden. This is like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says the entire field must be examined, for perhaps this is a different grave and the one that was lost has not yet been found.
gershom:b16.1: And Rabbi Yosei, who says let it be investigated, holds like Rabbi: since he found it, it is the one that became mixed.
gershom:b17.1: Rabbi Asi would say to you: with regard to impurity, even the first tanna concedes that once he reached bedrock it is pure, for one may say a raven or a mouse took it. But with a blemished animal, where he examined and did not find it, even Rabbi Yosei concedes that they are forbidden, for where would the blemished animal have gone?
gershom:b18.1: And the other, Rabbi Ḥiyya, would say to you: perhaps it was a temporary blemish and it healed.
gershom:b19.1: Since they were examined and stand [whole], and a blemished animal became mixed with them and was found, do we presume that these examined animals are apt to develop a blemish? Therefore it is not comparable to “let the entire field be examined.”
gershom:b20.1: A blemish is common among them: even though they were examined at the outset.
